_comment: The leak corpus is PhiGate's privacy proof.
Each case carries a payload plus the exact substrings that must NOT survive
redaction. TestLeakCorpus asserts that none of them appear in the redacted
output. If someone loosens a rule, reorders priorities, or reintroduces the
sequential-regex bug that used to corrupt overlapping matches, this fails.
'must_survive' pins the opposite property: text that must NOT be masked, so
the corpus also guards against a rule becoming so broad it destroys the
_secrets_note: Every credential below is synthetic and has never been issued. Even so, they
are stored as FRAGMENTS and joined at load time, so no credential-shaped
literal ever exists in a file in this repository.
That is not cosmetic. A test fixture that looks like a live Slack token is
indistinguishable from one to a secret scanner: GitHub push protection blocks
the push, and gitleaks/trufflehog fail the CI of anyone who forks this repo.
A corpus that cannot be committed is a corpus nobody runs, and this one is the
evidence behind PhiGate's central privacy claim — it has to stay runnable.
Reference a fragment set from a payload or a must_not_leak entry as ${name}.
TestNoLiteralCredentialsInCorpus enforces the rule for future contributors.
AWS's values are the ones published in AWS's own documentation and are
allowlisted by every scanner, but they are fragmented too so the rule stays
simple: no exceptions, nothing to judge case by case.

cases.name: aws_credentials_in_env_dump
cases.why: The original sequential-regex masker let the unix_path rule eat the middle of the secret key, emitting a partially masked value that looked safe.

cases.name: database_connection_string
cases.why: Passwords embedded in DSNs are the most common credential in a real stack trace.

cases.name: kv_secrets_in_config
cases.why: key=value credentials in application config pasted into a prompt.

cases.name: pem_private_key
cases.payload:
deploy failed, key is:
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
${pem_body}
RK+Lh9x5eJPo5CAZ3/ANBE0sTK0ZsDGMak2m1g7oruI3dY3VHqIxFTz0Ta1d+NAj
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
any ideas?
cases.why: A whole PEM block must go, not just the base64 lines.

cases.name: jwt_in_request_log
cases.why: A JWT payload is only base64; leaking one discloses every claim, here a person's name.

cases.name: github_and_slack_tokens
cases.payload: CI broke. GITHUB_TOKEN=${github_token} and slack hook token ${slack_token}
cases.why: SaaS tokens pasted from CI logs.

cases.name: llm_provider_key
cases.why: PhiGate proxies these keys itself; one leaking through a prompt compromises the gateway's own upstream account.

cases.name: jp_mynumber_in_ticket
cases.payload: 問い合わせ: 従業員の個人番号 1234 5678 9018 が給与システムに登録できません。
cases.why: 特定個人情報 under the My Number Act. This must never reach a cloud LLM under any routing decision.

cases.name: jp_customer_record
cases.payload: 顧客: 〒100-0001 東京都千代田区千代田1-1 電話 090-1234-5678 メール taro@example.co.jp カード 4111-1111-1111-1111
must_not_leak: 東京都千代田区千代田1-1
cases.why: A full Japanese customer record: postal code, address, phone, email and a Luhn-valid card. These are the universally-published test values, not fragments, because no scanner treats them as live credentials.

cases.name: internal_topology
cases.why: Internal hostnames disclose topology more usefully to an attacker than the IPs do. Requires PHIGATE_INTERNAL_DOMAINS to be configured; the corpus runs the engine with corp/internal set.

cases.name: unknown_bespoke_token
cases.why: No shipped pattern knows this format. The entropy detector is the safety net beneath the rules.

cases.name: azure_storage_connection_string
cases.why: Azure connection strings are pasted constantly in JP enterprise support tickets.

cases.name: clean_ops_question
cases.payload: nginx worker processes keep restarting after we enabled gzip. Where should I look first?
cases.why: The inverse property: an ordinary operator question must pass through untouched. A rule set that masks this destroys answer quality.
